title: An occult wrist fracture
prompt: A 23-year-old man falls onto his outstretched hand while skating. He has focal anatomic snuffbox tenderness and pain with gripping. Initial wrist radiographs show no fracture. Which approach best addresses the suspected injury?
options: Begin forceful wrist manipulation before reassessment
Exclude fracture unless the wrist is visibly deformed
Immobilize the wrist and arrange further imaging or timely reassessment
Allow unrestricted activity because the radiograph is normal
Diagnose a complete scapholunate tear solely from snuffbox tenderness
answer: Immobilize the wrist and arrange further imaging or timely reassessment
explanation: An initially occult scaphoid fracture remains possible; a normal first radiograph does not safely exclude it.

distractorExplanations.Immobilize the wrist and arrange further: An initially occult scaphoid fracture remains possible; a normal first radiograph does not safely exclude it.
distractorExplanations.Allow unrestricted activity because the: The clinical suspicion remains despite an initially normal film.
distractorExplanations.Diagnose a complete scapholunate tear so: That finding does not establish a specific ligament tear.
distractorExplanations.Begin forceful wrist manipulation before: This may worsen an unrecognized fracture.
distractorExplanations.Exclude fracture unless the wrist is vis: Scaphoid fractures can occur without obvious deformity.

title: Proximal fragment viability
prompt: A 29-year-old woman sustains a fracture through the scaphoid waist after a fall onto an extended wrist. At follow-up, the surgeon explains why the proximal fragment requires careful monitoring for impaired viability. Which anatomic feature best explains this concern?
options: The scaphoid is supplied only by the ulnar nerve
Much of the proximal scaphoid blood supply travels from distal entry points
The scaphoid has no blood supply before injury
All blood enters the proximal pole and flows distally
The proximal fragment is supplied exclusively by synovial fluid
answer: Much of the proximal scaphoid blood supply travels from distal entry points
explanation: A fracture can interrupt the blood supply reaching the proximal fragment.

distractorExplanations.Much of the proximal scaphoid blood supp: A fracture can interrupt the blood supply reaching the proximal fragment.
distractorExplanations.The scaphoid has no blood supply before: It has a blood supply, but the distribution makes some fragments vulnerable.
distractorExplanations.All blood enters the proximal pole and f: This reverses the clinically important pattern.
distractorExplanations.The proximal fragment is supplied exclus: Synovial fluid is not the primary blood supply to the bone.
distractorExplanations.The scaphoid is supplied only by the uln: Nerves do not provide the arterial perfusion described.

title: Selecting additional imaging
prompt: A 34-year-old cyclist has persistent radial-sided wrist pain after a fall. The examination remains suspicious for a scaphoid fracture, but the first radiographs are unrevealing. Which imaging test can identify an occult fracture before it becomes visible on repeat plain films?
options: MRI of the wrist
Repeat the identical radiographic views immediately
Stress radiographs of the scapholunate interval
Ultrasound limited to the first dorsal tendon compartment
Radiographs of the opposite wrist alone
explanation: MRI can reveal a scaphoid fracture that is occult on initial radiographs.

distractorExplanations.MRI of the wrist: MRI can reveal a scaphoid fracture that is occult on initial radiographs.
distractorExplanations.Repeat the identical radiographic views: An immediate identical study can remain negative; it does not provide MRI sensitivity to an occult injury.
distractorExplanations.Stress radiographs of the scapholunate i: These assess dynamic ligament instability rather than being the preferred test for an occult scaphoid fracture.
distractorExplanations.Ultrasound limited to the first dorsal t: This evaluates tendons rather than reliably excluding a scaphoid fracture.
distractorExplanations.Radiographs of the opposite wrist alone: Comparison anatomy cannot establish or exclude an occult fracture in the injured wrist.

title: Assessing fracture geometry
prompt: A 41-year-old man has a visible scaphoid waist fracture on radiographs. Before choosing treatment, the surgeon wants a clearer assessment of fragment displacement and the fracture configuration. Which additional study is particularly useful for this purpose?
options: Bone scintigraphy
Ultrasound of the flexor tendons
MR angiography of the forearm arteries
Repeat examination without additional imaging
CT of the wrist
explanation: CT provides detailed bony assessment of fracture geometry and displacement.

distractorExplanations.CT of the wrist: CT provides detailed bony assessment of fracture geometry and displacement.
distractorExplanations.Bone scintigraphy: It can detect increased bone turnover but does not define fragment geometry as precisely as CT.
distractorExplanations.Ultrasound of the flexor tendons: This is not the best study of scaphoid fracture displacement.
distractorExplanations.MR angiography of the forearm arteries: Large-vessel imaging does not answer the question of fracture geometry.
distractorExplanations.Repeat examination without additional im: Examination alone cannot quantify the fracture displacement.

title: Persistent nonunion
prompt: A 37-year-old construction worker reports chronic wrist pain and reduced motion months after an untreated scaphoid injury. Imaging shows persistent nonunion with degenerative change around the wrist. Which long-term complication is most consistent with this course?
options: De Quervain tenosynovitis
Isolated median nerve entrapment
Primary inflammatory polyarthritis
Post-traumatic wrist arthritis
Kienbock disease
explanation: Unhealed scaphoid injury can disrupt wrist mechanics and lead to degenerative change.

distractorExplanations.Post-traumatic wrist arthritis: Unhealed scaphoid injury can disrupt wrist mechanics and lead to degenerative change.
distractorExplanations.Kienbock disease: This concerns avascular necrosis of the lunate, rather than degenerative change secondary to scaphoid nonunion.
distractorExplanations.De Quervain tenosynovitis: This involves the first dorsal tendon compartment and does not explain the nonunion-associated joint degeneration.
distractorExplanations.Isolated median nerve entrapment: Nerve compression may cause sensory symptoms but does not explain this structural radiographic pattern.
distractorExplanations.Primary inflammatory polyarthritis: The localized degenerative findings following an unhealed fracture favor a post-traumatic process.
